tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.

   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Commit message here.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file outside the working directory, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

tools.name: SubagentHandback

Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position

- `next_page` - page number to request next

- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them

1	---
2	name: ingest-book
3	description: >-
4	  Ingest a book (PDF/EPUB full-text, Kindle highlights, or framework-only from a
5	  physical book) into the SecondBrain library as atomized, citable advisor entries. Use
6	  when the user wants to "ingest a book", "add a book to my library/advisors",
7	  "/ingest-book", or points at a book file for the advisor system. Do not use for
8	  articles, transcripts, or general resources (use ingest-resource).
9	argument-hint: "[book file or title] [domain]"
10	---
11	
12	# Ingest Book
13	
14	Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.
15	
16	**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
17	**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
18	**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
19	Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.
20	
21	## Model split (cost vs quality)
22	
23	This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
24	- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
25	  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
26	- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
27	  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
28	- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
29	  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
30	  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
31	  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
32	  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
33	  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
34	  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
35	  doesn't compound across the book.
36	
37	## Schema for every entry note
38	
39	Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.
40	
41	```yaml
42	---
43	type: library-entry
44	kind: principle
45	domain: <domain-slug>
46	book: <book-slug>
47	chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
48	topic: <2-5 word topic>
49	category: [tag, tag]
50	confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
51	ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
52	created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
53	---
54	
55	# <Human title of the idea>
56	
57	**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
58	**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
59	**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
60	**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
61	**Example** — one concrete instance.
62	```
63	
64	**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
65	framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.
66	
67	## Phase 1 — Intake
68	
69	1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
70	2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
71	3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
72	4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
73	   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
74	   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
75	   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.
76	
77	`_book.md` template:
78	```markdown
79	---
80	type: book-index
81	book: <book-slug>
82	title: <full title>
83	author: <author>
84	domain: <domain-slug>
85	ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
86	source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
87	created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
88	---
89	
90	# <title> — ingest map
91	
92	| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
93	|---|---------|--------|---------|
94	| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
95	```
96	
97	## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)
98	
99	**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
100	- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
101	  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
102	  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
103	  confidence entries from a scanned file.
104	- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`, where A and B are
105	  0-based PDF indexes and the range is inclusive: `--pages 12-20` returns 9 pages). Each page
106	  comes back with `page` (0-based index) and `viewer_page` (what a PDF viewer shows, index + 1).
107	  Cite pages one way throughout a book and state the convention in `_book.md`. For each:
108	  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
109	- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
110	  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.
111	
112	**Kindle highlights:**
113	- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
114	  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
115	- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".
116	
117	**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
118	- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
119	  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
120	  confidence ≤ untested.
121

123

---
name: ingest-book
description: >-
  Ingest a book (PDF/EPUB full-text, Kindle highlights, or framework-only from a
  physical book) into the SecondBrain library as atomized, citable advisor entries. Use
  when the user wants to "ingest a book", "add a book to my library/advisors",
  "/ingest-book", or points at a book file for the advisor system. Do not use for
  articles, transcripts, or general resources (use ingest-resource).
argument-hint: "[book file or title] [domain]"
---

# Ingest Book

Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.

**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.

## Model split (cost vs quality)

This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
  doesn't compound across the book.

## Schema for every entry note

Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.

```yaml
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: <domain-slug>
book: <book-slug>
chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
topic: <2-5 word topic>
category: [tag, tag]
confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <Human title of the idea>

**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
**Example** — one concrete instance.
```

**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.

## Phase 1 — Intake

1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.

`_book.md` template:
```markdown
---
type: book-index
book: <book-slug>
title: <full title>
author: <author>
domain: <domain-slug>
ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <title> — ingest map

| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|--------|---------|
| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
```

## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)

**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
  confidence entries from a scanned file.
- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`, where A and B are
  0-based PDF indexes and the range is inclusive: `--pages 12-20` returns 9 pages). Each page
  comes back with `page` (0-based index) and `viewer_page` (what a PDF viewer shows, index + 1).
  Cite pages one way throughout a book and state the convention in `_book.md`. For each:
  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.

**Kindle highlights:**
- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".

**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
  confidence ≤ untested.

## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)

- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.

## Phase 4 — Close-out

1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
   if an advisor exists.
4. Run `memsearch index "<vault_library>"` using the selected platform config
   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
5. Commit the vault using `vault_root` from the selected platform config: `git -C "<vault_root>" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.

## Rules
- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.

1	# Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)
2	
3	Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
4	Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
5	Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
6	Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").
7	
8	## How the source was checked
9	
10	- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
11	- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).
12	- What the images settled: Table 3.10 rows are labelled "I-III" and "MS"; at 67.5 kg MS is 13.1 vs I-III 13.0 (MS higher). Table 3.12 caption reads "kcalories"; front squat elite is 12.7. Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
13	- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398, dated July 2011; cochrane.org displays the same pub3 as "2022, Issue 4"), results via cochrane.org and the Authors' conclusions via the Europe PMC record; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
14	- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. Relevant stretching items found: `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...` (stretching did not improve DOMS or fatigue, p. 11), `research-papers/carvalho-2012-...` and `research-papers/chatzopoulos-2014-...` (acute stretching mode effects), Moyer `heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint` and `heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint` (active-passive gap), `research-papers/collings-2026-...` (non-contact ACL mechanism).
15	- All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).
16	- Rule 3: one `proven` (stretch-reflex framework), one `contested` (stretching benefits), four `untested` (no-unsafe-stretch, Olympic lifters, dedicated-stretching, spinal ligaments), the other 30 `supported`.
17	
18	## Global findings (rows cite "G1" etc.)
19	
20	- **G1. Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). Rows mark these "locator only" so they can be batched.
21	- **G2. Voice.** "The authors" is used throughout, which the brief allows. But 3.5-3.7 is clearly Siff's text: printed 180 (PDF 191) calls the section "this article", and printed 198 (PDF 209) says "a myotensiometer, which we used ... (Siff, 1986)". Where an entry rests on Siff (1986) or Siff (1987), say it is the author citing his own work. This matters for confidence in the Olympic-lifters, six-parameters and flexibility-definition entries.
22	- **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).
23	- **G4. "The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). Only the source's words may sit under that label; the rest needs "Inference:".
24	- **G5. Source contradictions not recorded** (each is in its row): Table 3.10 vs printed 168 text; breathing volumes vs the "exhalation always exceeded inhalation" statement (printed 172); Iashvili vs Tumanyan on static stretching and active flexibility (printed 175, 185 vs 186); stretch tolerance with tissue "unaltered" (printed 181) vs elastic/plastic tissue change (printed 176, 179, 180, 181); stretching benefits and warm-up injury claims (printed 163, 176, 185) vs "many athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up ... without suffering injury" (printed 192); Fig 3.34 separating ballistic from PNF vs the text making gentle ballistic a PNF subtype (printed 183, 186); triceps stretch text (printed 189) vs its own Figs 3.37 and 3.44; "prior stretching decreases isometric force" (printed 184) vs the force enhancement after stretch in the paper it cites.
25	- **G6. Baseline unused.** No entry cites `docs/method-baseline.md`. Not a defect, and better than misuse. Optional: the baseline line "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated ... an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention" (Inferred, class-1 transcript p.4) fits When to apply in the stretching-benefits and dedicated-stretching entries.
26	- **G7. "contested" as a category tag.** `claim--multiarticular-...` (confidence `supported`) and `claim--olympic-lifters-...` (confidence `untested`) carry `contested` in `category`. The brief treats contested as a confidence value that needs a named reason. Either drop the tag or set `confidence: contested` with a reason.
27	- **Improvement over the Ch2-3a batch:** Examples are almost all labelled "Inference:", no inline em dashes, no misused baseline lines. The remaining problems are misreads, locators, unrecorded contradictions and a few unlabeled mechanisms.
28	
29	## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)
30	
31	The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:
32	
33	1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
34	2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
35	3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).
36	
37	## Entry table
38	
39	| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |

41	| `claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance` | FIX (heavy) | Checked: jaw example, overflow/irradiation (Knott & Voss 1968), cross-training citations, dominance mechanism (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya 1955), Vinogradov 1966 factors, 25-33% (Mukhammedova), at PDF 177-178 / printed 166-167. (4) Omits the amortisation reactive-force figure ("by an average of 25% in the vertical jump", printed 167). (5) G3: no When to apply section. # Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").

## How the source was checked

- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).
- What the images settled: Table 3.10 rows are labelled "I-III" and "MS"; at 67.5 kg MS is 13.1 vs I-III 13.0 (MS higher). Table 3.12 caption reads "kcalories"; front squat elite is 12.7. Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398, dated July 2011; cochrane.org displays the same pub3 as "2022, Issue 4"), results via cochrane.org and the Authors' conclusions via the Europe PMC record; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. Relevant stretching items found: `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...` (stretching did not improve DOMS or fatigue, p. 11), `research-papers/carvalho-2012-...` and `research-papers/chatzopoulos-2014-...` (acute stretching mode effects), Moyer `heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint` and `heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint` (active-passive gap), `research-papers/collings-2026-...` (non-contact ACL mechanism).
- All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).
- Rule 3: one `proven` (stretch-reflex framework), one `contested` (stretching benefits), four `untested` (no-unsafe-stretch, Olympic lifters, dedicated-stretching, spinal ligaments), the other 30 `supported`.

## Global findings (rows cite "G1" etc.)

- **G1. Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). Rows mark these "locator only" so they can be batched.
- **G2. Voice.** "The authors" is used throughout, which the brief allows. But 3.5-3.7 is clearly Siff's text: printed 180 (PDF 191) calls the section "this article", and printed 198 (PDF 209) says "a myotensiometer, which we used ... (Siff, 1986)". Where an entry rests on Siff (1986) or Siff (1987), say it is the author citing his own work. This matters for confidence in the Olympic-lifters, six-parameters and flexibility-definition entries.
- **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).
- **G4. "The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). Only the source's words may sit under that label; the rest needs "Inference:".
- **G5. Source contradictions not recorded** (each is in its row): Table 3.10 vs printed 168 text; breathing volumes vs the "exhalation always exceeded inhalation" statement (printed 172); Iashvili vs Tumanyan on static stretching and active flexibility (printed 175, 185 vs 186); stretch tolerance with tissue "unaltered" (printed 181) vs elastic/plastic tissue change (printed 176, 179, 180, 181); stretching benefits and warm-up injury claims (printed 163, 176, 185) vs "many athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up ... without suffering injury" (printed 192); Fig 3.34 separating ballistic from PNF vs the text making gentle ballistic a PNF subtype (printed 183, 186); triceps stretch text (printed 189) vs its own Figs 3.37 and 3.44; "prior stretching decreases isometric force" (printed 184) vs the force enhancement after stretch in the paper it cites.
- **G6. Baseline unused.** No entry cites `docs/method-baseline.md`. Not a defect, and better than misuse. Optional: the baseline line "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated ... an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention" (Inferred, class-1 transcript p.4) fits When to apply in the stretching-benefits and dedicated-stretching entries.
- **G7. "contested" as a category tag.** `claim--multiarticular-...` (confidence `supported`) and `claim--olympic-lifters-...` (confidence `untested`) carry `contested` in `category`. The brief treats contested as a confidence value that needs a named reason. Either drop the tag or set `confidence: contested` with a reason.
- **Improvement over the Ch2-3a batch:** Examples are almost all labelled "Inference:", no inline em dashes, no misused baseline lines. The remaining problems are misreads, locators, unrecorded contradictions and a few unlabeled mechanisms.

## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)

The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:

1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).

Tensing the flexors of the left arm has no effect in this case" (printed 167). (3) Entry says the 8-22% decrease happens "without prior right-arm fatigue"; source gives it "during rhythmic flexing of the right arm", no fatigue condition stated. (4) Omits the amortisation reactive-force figure ("by an average of 25% in the vertical jump", printed 167). (5) G3: no When to apply section. (6) Locator "PDF p. 177, printed p. 166"; content runs to PDF 178 / printed 167. After fatiguing the right flexors, tensing the left extensors raised work capacity; tensing the left flexors had no effect. Mukhammedova (1958): left-extensor contraction raised right-flexor strength and speed more than left-flexor contraction; the largest effect came when the additional effort was 25-33% of the right arm's." ### `_book.md` (not in the 36 count): FIX

Entry counts per row match the 36 files (8 for 3.4.3-3.4.10, 28 for 3.5-3.7; "60" for Ch3 is right). The 3.4.4 "0 entries" dedup note is acceptable, but name the entries it defers to (Ch3a `claim--pre-working-muscle-state-ranks-performance`, Ch1 `principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy`).

## Missing (important ideas in printed 166-200 that no entry captures)

1. **"Isolation" is load-dependent (printed 198 / PDF 209).** "The greater the load, the greater the overflow and the greater the involvement of other muscle groups"; isolation by electrical stimulation, low load or loadless training "generally develops more muscle hypertrophy than functional strength"; palpation versus EMG or myotensiometer (Siff 1986). This ties the irradiation entry (3.4.3) to exercise selection (3.7).
2. **Overtraining is not an energy sum (printed 170 / PDF 181).** Overload vs overuse types; "a workout consisting of a few maximal attempts may elicit an overload type of overtraining far more readily than a much longer workout ... with moderate weights"; overload may come more from technique that raises stress (force per unit area); actual work is 5-12 min of a 1.5-2.5 h session.
3. **The other reflexes (printed 178-179 / PDF 189-190).** Crossed extensor reflex 0.2-0.5 s later, relevant to unilateral dumbbell work; reciprocal inhibition; rebound making repeated maximal acyclic efforts harder but cyclic ones easier; local muscle spasm as a "physiological splint", sometimes relieved by contracting the opposite muscle with the joint fixed.
4. **Multi-directional and rotational stretching (printed 181, 186 / PDF 192, 197).** Collagen fibre orientation differs by tissue, so stretching should be multi-directional; "very few rotational stretches about the longitudinal axes of the limbs are ever used"; PNF spiral-diagonal patterns give "superior three-dimensional functional ROM". Plus printed 175 (PDF 186): ROM in one direction depends on concurrent movement in another, so single-plane lab ROM measures are equivocal.
5. **Hormonal state and stretching (printed 183 / PDF 194).** Pregnancy, menstruation and exogenous hormones (anabolic steroids, cortisone) change collagen mechanics, "so that stretching techniques should be adjusted accordingly (Viidik, 1973)". The book's only cited steroid-collagen statement; relevant to the steroid entry and to Athletic Medicine.

## Overall verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** Counts over the 36 scoped entries: **GO 5, FIX 31, NO-GO 0.** Plus `_book.md` FIX.

Verdict rule applied: NO-GO only where the title or headline reverses or misreports the source. Two entries have reversed or wrong physiology in the body (irradiation: flexors/extensors and the Popov/Mukhammedova attribution; history dependence: "prior stretching decreases isometric force" presented as well known); both headlines hold, so both are heavy FIXes.

Fix before promotion:

1. Heavy rewrites: `claim--irradiation-...` (Popov vs Mukhammedova numbers, extensors not flexors after fatigue, add When to apply) and `claim--stretch-shortening-history-dependence-...` (restate from the Herzog & Leonard abstract; force enhancement after stretch; "perhaps"; cat soleus; label the transfer to jumps).
2. Scope `proven` in `framework--stretch-reflex-types-...` to the replicated core, mark the Guyton-specific claims not proven, and rewrite When to apply so it no longer contradicts Basmajian's EMG silence (printed 177-178).
3. Correct factual misreads: Table 3.10 "I-III" and the 67.5 kg exception; biceps "abducted" and obliques "flexion" (stretching matrix); "which limb" (positive supportive reaction); flexibility-speed "static and dynamic"; "acute exposure" (ligament Example); "valuable" vs "invaluable"; "each from a single citation" (hypnosis); weightlifting vs depth-jump (instruction); cold "not as pre-exercise preparation"; Olympic-lifters context; coach guidance (blindfold); javelinists.
4. Record the source contradictions listed in G5, each with both pages.
5. Confidence: set the steroid clause `untested` (or split); keep the cycling/push-up/sit-up recommendation flagged uncited and `untested`; add Lauersen 2014 or Herbert & Gabriel 2002 (verify) and Dupuy 2018 (vault) to the stretching-benefits contested reason.
6. Locators (G1, batchable): soft-tissue, six-parameters, stretch-tolerance, reflex-techniques, spurious-tension, relaxation methods, irradiation, hypnosis, spinal ligaments, movement matrix, ligament adaptation; and the `_book.md` rows.
7. Labels (G4 and rows): "Inference:" on the unlabeled mechanisms and applications named in the rows (four-methods, ballistic, joint stabilization, spinal ligaments, soft-tissue, stretch-tolerance, Valsalva blood pressure, flexibility qualities, taxonomy Example, no-unsafe-stretch Example, movement-matrix Example, spurious-tension Example, six-parameters Example). Add When to apply to the irradiation and hypnosis entries (G3). Note Siff self-citations (G2).
8. Related links to add: Moyer active-passive entries (active-flexibility, eccentric quasi-isometrics), Ch1 S-factors (flexibility qualities), Ch1 SEC/PEC (stretch tolerance tension), Ch3a pelvic tilt (spinal ligaments), Myszka constraints entries (instruction, as tension), Dupuy 2018 (stretching benefits), Carvalho 2012 and Chatzopoulos 2014 (taxonomy), collings-2026 (joint stabilization).
