- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]
- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]

## Education and staff development

- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]
- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]

---

## No material found

None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.

---

## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

14	# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics
15	
16	**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).
17	
18	**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
19	- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
20	- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
21	- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
22	- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
23	- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).
24	
25	**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."
26	
27	*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*
28	
29	**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.
30	
31	**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.
32	
33	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.
34	
35	**Example** — Screening question for a strong but non-reactive athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.
36	
37	**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics

**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).

**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).

**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."

*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*

**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.

**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.

**Example** — Screening question for a strong but non-reactive athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.

**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

"""Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python scripts/lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STAGING = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
            link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
            if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                issues.append(f"unresolved [[{link}]]")
        if not f.name.startswith("_"):
            m = re.search(r"^confidence:\s*(\S+)", text, re.M)
            if not m or m.group(1).strip("\"'") not in CONF:
                issues.append(f"confidence={m.group(1) if m else 'missing'}")
            for s in SECTIONS:
                if s not in text:
                    issues.append(f"missing {s}")
            h = HISTORY.findall(text)
            if h:
                issues.append(f"review-history words {sorted(set(x.lower() for x in h))}")
        if issues:
            problems += len(issues)
            print(f"{f.parent.name}/{f.name}: " + "; ".join(issues))

12	---
13	
14	# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed
15	
16	**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
17	inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
18	constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
19	beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
20	high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
21	"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
22	different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
23	maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
24	strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
25	this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
26	38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
27	gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
28	Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
31	isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
32	that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
33	cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
34	conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
35	used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
36	modern profiling.
37	
38	**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
39	the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to

# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works** — The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
modern profiling.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
frameworks are equivalent. The text itself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as not
universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
(Sutarno & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19): the model is a strong generalization,
not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

"""Extract a PDF into per-page text as JSON, and detect scanned/image PDFs.
Usage: python extract_pdf.py <book.pdf> [--pages A-B] [--probe]
Prefers pypdf; if absent, attempts pip install into user site at runtime.
--probe prints {"pages": N, "text_pages": K, "scanned": bool} and exits.
Page numbering (read this before citing pages):
- "page" is the 0-based PDF index (the first PDF page is 0). It stays 0-based so
  citations written by earlier ingests remain valid.
- "viewer_page" is page + 1: the number a PDF viewer and the Read tool show.
- --pages A-B takes 0-based indexes and is INCLUSIVE of both ends: --pages 12-20
  returns indexes 12 through 20 (9 pages). Before 2026-09-26 the end was exclusive,
  which silently dropped the last page of every range.
"""
import sys, json, subprocess

def _ensure_pypdf():
    try:
        import pypdf  # noqa
        return
    except ImportError:
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--quiet", "--user", "pypdf"], check=False)

def load(path):
    _ensure_pypdf()
    from pypdf import PdfReader
    return PdfReader(path)

def page_texts(reader):
    out = []
    for pg in reader.pages:
        try: out.append(pg.extract_text() or "")
        except Exception: out.append("")
    return out

def main():
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    if not args:
        print("usage: extract_pdf.py <book.pdf> [--pages A-B] [--probe]", file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(2)
    path = args[0]
    reader = load(path)
    texts = page_texts(reader)
    if "--probe" in args:
        text_pages = sum(1 for t in texts if len(t.strip()) > 40)
        n = len(texts)
        scanned = n > 0 and (text_pages / n) < 0.2
        print(json.dumps({"pages": n, "text_pages": text_pages, "scanned": scanned}))
        return
    lo, hi = 0, len(texts)
    if "--pages" in args:
        rng = args[args.index("--pages") + 1]
        a, b = rng.split("-")
        lo, hi = int(a), int(b)
    # Inclusive end (fixed 2026-09-26; it was exclusive and dropped the last page).
    print(json.dumps([{"page": i, "viewer_page": i + 1, "text": texts[i]}
                      for i in range(max(lo, 0), min(hi + 1, len(texts)))], ensure_ascii=False))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

SUPERTRAINING
THE MEANS OF SPECIAL 
STRENGTH TRAINING
Opinion concerning the means and methods of strength training often repeats itself, with the beginning of the 
modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the 
means of strength training more precisely. However, with the improvement in sporting achievements, the effect 
of these means became less marked. The volume of the same exercises was increased, but it was found that this 
approach also has its limitations (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Once again, researchers turned to analysis of sports 
movements, now equipped with better measuring technology.
This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example, 
when information regarding the significance of strength in sport emerged from the laboratory and coaches looked 
optimistically to weight training. The next trend was towards specificity, since studies indicated that the strength 
necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this 
specificity of strength turned attention to the principle of selectivity in the

=== PAGE 213 viewer 214 ===

question: "How should peaking and tapering work across an in-season collegiate American football schedule?"
-status: draft (awaiting Eric's review)
+status: draft rev 2 (review applied 2026-09-27; awaiting Eric's review)
+review: docs/synthesis/_work/review_peaking_synthesis_opus.md
sources:
- Issurin, Block Periodization (2008 book)
- Bompa, Periodization (Ch 1-2)
- Verkhoshansky and Siff, Supertraining
-  - Bondarchuk, Transfer of Training in Sports
- Evans, Elite Sports Performance (course slides)

- Stokes et al. 2020; Afonso et al. 2019; Cosio et al. 2026; Norris et al. 2019; Gathercole et al. 2015; Heishman et al. 2020; McCall et al. 2023; Impellizzeri et al. 2020; Galiano et al. 2026; Claudino et al. 2016
- Football: Aychman et al. 2026; Lewis (dissertation); Lever et al. 2026; Merrigan et al. 2022; Iosia et al. 2008; Wellman et al. 2019; Hoffman et al. 2003; Peterson (dissertation)

-  - External: Bosquet et al. 2007; Mujika and Padilla 2003; Vachon et al. 2021; Marrier et al. 2017; Pritchard et al. 2015, 2019; Haugen et al. 2019; Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009; Ronnestad et al. 2011; Spiering et al. 2021; Cuthbert et al. 2024; Mujika and Padilla 2000 (Part I); Ross and Leveritt 2001; Saldanha et al. 2026

+  - External: Bosquet et al. 2007, 2013; Mujika and Padilla 2003; Vachon et al. 2021; Marrier et al. 2017; Pritchard et al. 2015, 2019; Haugen et al. 2019; Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009; Ronnestad et al. 2011; Spiering et al. 2021; Cuthbert et al. 2024; Mujika and Padilla 2000 (Part I); Ross and Leveritt 2001; Saldanha et al. 2026
# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule
## 1. The question

-As asked: how should we peak and taper for in-season college football? In practice it splits into four questions. What does a normal game week look like as a small taper? How long does each quality last without exposure, so what has to be touched every week? How should Applied Performance read readiness in game week? What do we do in the few windows with no game: bye weeks, camp to week 1, and the postseason gap?

+As asked: how should we peak and taper for in-season college football? It splits four ways: what a normal game week looks like as a small taper; how long each quality lasts without exposure; how to read readiness in game week; and what to do in game-free windows (bye weeks, camp to week 1, the postseason gap).

-The sources mostly answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library was built on single-event or discrete-meet sports: kayakers ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported]), one swimmer ([[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]] [untested]), throwers ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported]). Football plays 12 or more weekly games and has no single peak. **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract) say taper research is concentrated in individual sports and single events and does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5) call sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic. The evidence ceiling is low: no study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when a model predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]], paper brief, pp. 1, 4). So this note treats the season as "hold readiness every week" and keeps "peak on purpose" for the rare game-free window.

+The sources mostly answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract) say taper research centres on individual sports and single events and does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5) call sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic. No study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when a model predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So this note treats the season as "hold readiness every week" and keeps "peak on purpose" for the rare game-free window.
## 2. Bottom line
-1. Keep a floor of one heavy lower-body strength session every game week, early in the week, with load kept high and sets cut. [supported direction; floor, not optimum; no football trial]

-2. Give every player one true max-velocity exposure every game week, planned rather than assumed from practice, with priority on positions that rarely reach top speed in games. [contested on the day count, supported on direction]

-3. Shape the week heavy-early and light-late: heaviest lifting and practice Tuesday and Wednesday, at least 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday on. [supported for the shape; descriptive only in college football]

-4. Read game-week readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, flight time to contraction time), no arm swing, against each player's own norm and split by position group and starter status. Do not rely on jump height alone or on ACWR. [supported direction; football samples are small]

-5. Save a real multi-day taper (about 1 to 2 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one planned peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]

+1. Every game week has two floors: one heavy lower-body session, load high and sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure for every player [contested; no football data]. Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games (no source tests this).

+2. Lift heaviest early in the week; for a Saturday game, hold the last high-volume practice no later than Wednesday and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday. [Issurin's template (rugby league, Baker 2001) and one D-I program agree on early-heavy, late-light; they differ on the heaviest practice day; descriptive only in college football] Inference: keep about 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, drawn from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak; no source tests a gap to kickoff.

+3. Read game-week readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's own norm, not from jump height alone or ACWR. These metrics are noisier than jump height, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; football samples are small] Inference: splitting by position group and starter status rests on off-season profiles and one exploratory study; no source sets game-week thresholds by group.
+4. Keep aerobic and repeat-effort conditioning in every week; it may be the quality lost fastest. [contested: Eric's baseline and Mujika and Padilla 2000 against Issurin's table]

+5. Save a real multi-day taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one planned peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]
## 3. Where the sources agree

-**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 105). Bondarchuk keeps strength exercises "to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level" ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported], PDF p. 175; track and field). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, mostly endurance): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, not in season): only the higher-intensity taper improved IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

+**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies; sports not listed in the abstract, mostly endurance per the evidence file): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): the tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity taper showed small effect-size gains in IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

-**Strength lasts; speed is fragile.** Issurin lists max strength at 30 ± 5 days and alactic speed at 5 ± 3 days after training stops, with no sample reported ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested], PDF p. 35). He grounds speed's short residual in "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" (same entry, PDF pp. 35-36). Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand, the only in-season figure in the library). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one session every two weeks lost both. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly general and younger adult populations): strength held up to 32 weeks on one session and one set per exercise per week if relative load was kept; the authors say data are too thin for athlete-specific advice. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 3): games give some stimulus but likely not enough to keep max speed.

+**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season week]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one every two weeks lost both; jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly younger general adults) found strength held up to 32 weeks on one set per exercise per week at kept relative load, but say the data are too thin for athlete advice.

-**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the in-season week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block, with 28 to 30 h between the last strength key-workout and the key practice ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: the worked week assumes a Sunday game, so a Saturday game moves it one day earlier. Low-frequency peripheral fatigue can last up to 48 h ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]] [supported], printed p. 15), and high volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). College data match the shape. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program): Tuesday was the planned high-load day, and in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned cut in duration while Thursday did not change (PDF p. 6). Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; Zotero PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices came closest to game demands for linemen.

+**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block. For a Sunday game: strength key-workouts Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, the week's key practice ("substantial or big" load) Thursday afternoon, 28 to 30 h after the last lift, and only the pre-game session load-restricted (same entry, PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: shifting one day earlier for a Saturday game gives lifts Monday and Tuesday mornings, key practice Wednesday afternoon, Thursday off, a light Friday. High volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned duration cut while Thursday did not change.

-**Fast force stays down for 3 to 4 days after a game.** After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a]], paper brief, p. 8; n = 9 regional players). After AFL matches, early RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down at 96 h while peak force barely moved, and the responsive metric was the noisiest (CV 16.4%) ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th]], paper brief, p. 2).

-**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height recovered by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football]], paper brief, pp. 96-97; n = 5 per CMJ study). At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time moved -0.7% while FT:CT fell 7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue]], paper brief, p. 7; n = 8). No-arm-swing CMJ suits acute readiness ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division]], paper brief, pp. 5-12; D-I basketball). ACWR offered no predictive advantage over an intercept-only model, leaving only "not too much too soon" ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).

+**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height fell only slightly by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed largely reduced ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; n = 5). At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time moved -0.7% while FT:CT fell 7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue|Gathercole 2015]], p. 7; n = 8). The cost is noise: several phase-duration and RFD variables failed reliability, FT:CT was less reliable with arm swing, and the study tested reliability, not sensitivity ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division|Heishman 2020]], pp. 5-12; D-I basketball). ACWR offered no predictive advantage over an intercept-only model ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor|Impellizzeri 2020]], pp. 4-5).
## 4. Where they disagree

-**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Three positions. Issurin: speed goes first, aerobic and strength last ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested]). Eric's class-4 slides: aerobic goes first, speed last (section 7). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I (abstract): under 4 weeks of reduced stimulus, highly trained athletes lose VO2max fast while strength losses are limited, which sides with class 4 on aerobic. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-professional soccer players, uncontrolled): after a 5-day break, max velocity and repeated-sprint time got worse while jump and thigh strength held, which sides with Issurin on speed. **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (Zotero, PDF p. 17): short-sprint losses are milder than expected, longer sprints suffer more. Inference: these may answer different questions (loss after full cessation versus loss under a small retention dose), so they should not be merged yet. What would settle it: our own sprint and CMJ data before and after bye weeks and winter break.

+**Where the heaviest practice sits, and the post-game window.** Issurin puts the key practice late (Wednesday after the Saturday shift). College data put it early: Wellman's program planned Tuesday as the highest practice load (PDF p. 6), and Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit inside the post-game window. After AFL matches, early IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down 17.8% at 72 h and 16.9% at 96 h while peak force barely moved, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2). After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control group). A Saturday game puts Monday at about 48 h, Tuesday about 72 h, Wednesday about 96 h. Unresolved: either the early-week lifts and practice load incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin's model), or heavy and high-velocity work waits until Wednesday. No source tests this in football. What would settle it: our CMJ and sprint data by hours since the game.

+**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Issurin's table: speed goes first (5 ± 3 days), aerobic and max strength last (30 ± 5), no sample reported, grounded in "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested], PDF pp. 35-36). **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic goes first, speed last. **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I (abstract): under 4 weeks of reduced stimulus, highly trained athletes lose VO2max fast while strength losses are limited. Inference: this sides with class 4 on aerobic. The residual entry adds that intense work does not prevent aerobic detraining during a taper (Mujika 1999, PDF p. 34). **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-professional soccer players, uncontrolled): after a 5-day break, repeated-sprint time and RAST peak velocity worsened (small to moderate) while jump and hip adductor and abductor strength held. Inference: this leans toward Issurin on speed, though RAST is not a max-velocity test. Against a short speed residual: **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (Zotero, PDF p. 17): short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated"; longer sprints suffer more. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2013 (abstract; meta-analysis, 103 studies, mixed populations): cessation cut maximal power least (SMD -0.20, against -0.46 for maximal force). Ronnestad (above) kept 40-m speed without dedicated max-velocity work. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 3) say games likely do not keep max speed, but cite Issurin for it. Inference, which the residual entry itself flags: these may answer different questions (full cessation versus a small retention dose). Issurin warns that a design built only on residual lengths "will be extremely rigid and inflexible" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin residual mini-blocks]] [supported], PDF p. 127). What would settle it: our sprint and CMJ data before and after bye weeks and winter break.

-**Heavy lifting close to competition (D-5, D-7).** Issurin reports both sides: Platonov and Fesenko 1990 (swimmers, volleyball, tennis) say heavy work before competition hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera 2003 say sport-specific strength work keeps the force component ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract; strength athletes): 2 to 4 days without lifting appears best for peak max strength. Inference: in a Saturday week that puts the last heavy lift on Tuesday or Wednesday. What would settle it: mRSI on game-day minus 1 by days since the last heavy lift.

+**Heavy lifting close to competition (D-5, D-7).** Issurin reports both sides: Platonov and Fesenko 1990 say heavy work before competition hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera 2003 say sport-specific strength work keeps the force component (Issurin pre-competitive, PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract; strength athletes): 2 to 4 days of training cessation appears optimal for peak max strength. Inference: a football week never stops training, so this bounds the last heavy lift rather than setting it; the shifted Issurin week puts it about 4 days out. What would settle it: mRSI on game-day minus 1 by days since the last heavy lift.

-**Maintain or build in season.** Ronnestad and Spiering say one session per week maintains. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshman players, n = 14 per group, two separate seasons, 2 sessions per week): a linear in-season program raised 1RM squat by 13.8 ± 7.4 kg while the nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles the second program, so verify the full text. Inference: building may be realistic for low-snap freshmen, not starters.

+**Maintain or build in season.** **External:** Ronnestad and Spiering (above) say one session per week maintains; Issurin's template uses two. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshman players, n = 14 per group, two separate seasons, 2 sessions per week): a linear in-season program raised 1RM squat by 13.8 ± 7.4 kg while the nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles the second program, so verify the full text. Inference: building may be realistic for low-snap freshmen, not starters.

-**Timing models (D-1, D-2).** Bompa's supercompensation windows ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] [supported], Ch 1) against Verkhoshansky's adaptive reconstruction, where timing "remains indeterminate" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] [contested], PDF pp. 94-99), and Evans calling the fitness-fatigue model "JUST A CONCEPT" ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]] [untested]). Inference: use them as mental models; do not schedule to the hour.

+**Timing models (D-1, D-2).** Bompa ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa supercompensation]] [supported], Ch 1), Verkhoshansky ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky adaptive reconstruction]] [contested], PDF pp. 94-99) and Evans ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans fitness-fatigue]] [untested]) disagree on whether adaptation timing can be predicted. Inference: use them as mental models; do not schedule to the hour.
## 5. What transfers and what does not

-**Transfers:** the direction of residual effects and a weekly re-exposure cadence for speed; the in-season two-mini-block week; keep intensity, cut volume; readiness monitoring with CMJ strategy metrics; the 72 to 96 h post-game window for fast-force work. Also that body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper with stable body mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; the primary abstract shows n = 16). Inference: linemen with high intake in a low-load window are most exposed.

+**Transfers:** the direction of residual effects and a weekly re-exposure cadence; the two-mini-block week as a template; keep intensity, cut volume; CMJ strategy metrics. Also that body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper at stable body mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization taper]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; triathletes, n = 16, no significance test reported). Inference: linemen with high intake in a low-load window are most exposed.

-**Does not transfer:** single-peak taper prescriptions. Issurin's 1 to 3 week realization block, the kayak race-simulation dosage, the 8 to 10 sessions per week camp figure, Bompa's 4 to 12 week delayed gain after concentrated loading ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] [supported], Ch 2), and the roughly 3% taper gain (**External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003, abstract) all assume one target event. A game week has no room for them.

+**Does not transfer:** single-peak prescriptions (Issurin's 1 to 3 week realization block, kayak dosages, 8 to 10 sessions per week, the 4 to 12 week delayed gain after concentrated loading (Siff and Verkhoshansky, cited by Bompa: [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa concentrated loading]] [supported], Ch 2), the roughly 3% taper gain in Mujika and Padilla 2003) assume one target event.

-**The exception:** one planned peak after game-free weeks, such as a bowl or a title game with a gap. **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (Zotero abstract only; 10 international rugby sevens players, 3-week taper after a 4-week camp): 70 to 80% of individual peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): tapering gave moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max, but the studies could not say which strategy is best. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): sprinters should expect smaller taper gains than endurance or strength athletes. Inference: for a bowl, run 1 to 2 weeks of reduced volume with speed and heavy lifting kept, and do not judge success from sprint times alone.

+**The exception:** one planned peak after game-free weeks, such as a bowl. **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (Zotero abstract only; 10 international rugby sevens players, 3-week taper after a 4-week camp): 70 to 80% of individual peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): tapering gave moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max, but no best strategy emerged. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): 2 to 3 weeks for strength and power sports, with smaller gains expected in sprinters. Fitness-fatigue modelling suggests accepted tapers "may be too rigorous and short" (Fitz-Clarke 1991, in Verkhoshansky taper timing, printed pp. 88-89). Inference: for a bowl, run 1 to 3 weeks of reduced volume with speed and heavy lifting kept, and do not judge success from sprint times alone.
## 6. What none of them covers

-- **Bye weeks.** No source prescribes one. Peterson (dissertation, grey literature, year and institution unverified; 108 D-I players, 2021 to 2023) found skill and mid-size players jumped better after the bye than at baseline while big players jumped worse, and the gap lasted to 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Inference: a bye may need position-specific dosing, and should still include one speed and one heavy exposure given Saldanha.

-- **Short weeks.** Only soccer load-ratio data, descriptive ([[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).

-- **Camp to week 1.** Wellman describes a deliberate duration cut in week 1 (PDF p. 6); the closest intervention is U17 futsal, n = 9 per group ([[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching]], paper brief).

-- **Postseason and the bowl gap.** All bowl-prep structure is Inference from kayak calendars. Nothing covers a title game followed by an uncertain bowl date or consecutive playoff games. For a long layoff, contact should rebuild over at least 3 to 4 weeks and high-speed running progressively ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports]], paper brief, p. 7; expert opinion, rugby).

-- **Position groups.** CMJ profiles differ by group ([[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a]], paper brief; off-season data) and game load differs by exposure ([[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football]], paper brief). Nothing says how dose should differ.

-- **Low-snap players.** Non-starters showed poorer recovery markers despite lower external load ([[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football]], paper brief, pp. 1, 9; 39 players, one program, exploratory). No source prescribes make-up loading.
-- **Detraining across a football season.** Only the secondhand 14 to 16 week figure.

+- **Bye weeks.** No source prescribes one. **External:** Peterson (dissertation, grey literature, year and institution unverified; 108 D-I players, 2021 to 2023) found a group x time interaction on a CMJ stretch-shortening factor: the gap between big players and skill or mid-size players widened after the bye and persisted 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Within-group change from baseline is not tested on that page. Inference: a bye may need position-specific dosing and should still include a speed or repeated-sprint exposure, given Saldanha.

None says how dose should differ.

+- **Postseason, the bowl gap, consecutive playoff games.** Bowl structure is Inference from kayak calendars. After a long layoff, contact should rebuild over at least 3 to 4 weeks ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports|Stokes 2020]], p. 7; expert opinion, rugby).
+- **Detraining across a season.** Only the secondhand 14 to 16 week figure and one in-season freshman strength study (Hoffman 2003); nothing on starters' speed or strength across a season.

## 7. Eric's baseline

-- **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the daily readiness marker, chosen over wellness surveys because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable" (method-baseline, SportSmith piece). Daily wellness surveys were dropped after about one year because athletes learned to game them. This agrees with section 3 on strategy metrics and with [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective]] (paper brief) on honest answering being a trust problem.

Opinion concerning the means and methods of strength training often repeats itself, with the beginning of the 
modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the 
means of strength training more precisely. However, with the improvement in sporting achievements, the effect 
of these means became less marked. The volume of the same exercises was increased, but it was found that this 
approach also has its limitations (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Once again, researchers turned to analysis of sports 
movements, now equipped with better measuring technology.
This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example, 
when information regarding the significance of strength in sport emerged from the laboratory and coaches looked 
optimistically to weight training. The next trend was towards specificity, since studies indicated that the strength 
necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this 
specificity of strength turned attention to the principle of selectivity in the means of special preparation.
In general, the progress of strength preparation methods leads logically to examination of the motor 
mechanisms underlying sports movements. This results in new hypotheses being formulated to replace currently 
accepted ones, beginning with an understanding of actual sports movements and the specific level of the athlete's 
physical fitness. Thus, one can understand why it is necessary to devise new means that cannot easily be rejected 
in favour of fashionable techniques which have become established more on the basis of tradition and emotion 
than on scientific grounds (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Thus, the selection of the strength and other training means based on the motor specifics of given sports 
exercises, is one of the most important tasks in sport. This has marked a turning point in training science, which 
has identified the progression of all training from a foundation of general physical preparation (GPP) to 
wbsequent specific physical preparation (SPP), guided by an intimate understanding of the specific character of 
the sports activity. The practice of selecting the means of strength preparation, based upon the specifics of the 
athlete's movements, leads one to abandon reliance on intuition alone and find a more objective foundation.
This foundation is expressed in the form of the principle of dynamic correspondence, which determines how 
closely the means of special strength preparation corresponds to the functioning of the neuromuscular system in a 
given sport (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
4.1 The Problem of Training Means
The process of adaptation involves stimulation from the external or internal environment, which leaves certain 
traces in the body. With repetitive stimulation the traces accumulate, leading to significant modifications which 
raise the functional capability of the body. A characteristic of every living creature is the relative speed with 
which it adapts to repetitive stimulation. The same regime of stimulation can rapidly produce habituation and 
then fail to elicit any further adaptation, only maintaining the existing levels. Another regime can prove excessive 
and lead to overtraining, which prevents adaptation. An optimum level of stimulation offered in a progressively 
increasing sequence of carefully chosen means is essential for ensuring adaptation at successively higher levels of 
performance (see 1.14).
This, in general and simplified terms, is the physiological foundation of training. In reality it is a very intricate 
process, since systematic exercise as a means of physical conditioning involves a complex of different stimuli 
which affect all systems of the body. For example, to successfully increase strength, the load, number of 
repetitions, tempo of execution and workout venue all influence the effectiveness of the training. These variables 
could be listed at great length, since the development of strength is not the only goal of training. However, 
besides this, it is likely that the coach will select from the vast number of variations, that combination of means 
which he considers will produce the greatest success.
4.1.1 Characteristics of Strength Increase
Strength as a specific result of physical adaptation is determined by the intensity and repetitiveness of the stimuli 
to which the body is exposed during use of the motor apparatus. Only a sufficiently intense level of muscular

contraction, which can be achieved in different ways (e.g. using isometric tension or heavy loads at low velocities), 
will provide an effective training stimulus. Research has shown that the threshold training stimulus necessary for 
increasing muscular strength in the average person should not be less than one-third of the maximal strength 
(Hettinger & Muller, 1953). As strength increases, the intensity of the stimulus required to produce a training 
effect should be increased, and reach 80-95% of the athlete's maximum. It may be appropriate that the strength of 
the training stimulus sometimes equals or even exceeds the level of the competition stimulus of the given exercise 
(Moroz, 1962; Ratov, 1962; Verkhoshansky, 1963).
Thus, the development of strength requires that the intensity of the stimulus be gradually increased. It was 
discovered that every stimulus has a specific strengthening threshold, the achievement of which fails to elicit any 
further increase in muscular strength (Muller, 1962). The less trained the muscles, the farther the strengthening 
threshold from the initial state. The rate at which strength increases from the initial level to the strengthening 
threshold, expressed as a percentage of the current maximum strength, is independent of sex, age, muscle group 
and the level of the strengthening threshold (Muller, 1962). After the strengthening threshold has been reached 
strength can be increased only by intensifying the training (e.g. by substituting stronger means, devising more 
effective combinations or increasing the volume of work).
These early attempts at establishing general principles need to be more precisely applied in terms of the 
means and methods of strength development, as well as the individual situation. For instance, according to 
Korobkov (1953), Gerasimov (1953) and Vasiliev (1954), strength increases relatively uniformly during the initial 
stages of training, independent of how the load is applied in training, whether large or small. Approximately 
equivalent increases in strength arc obtained with loads of 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% of maximum. An increase in 
the intensity of training in the initial stages (e.g. using a heavier load, faster tempo of movement and shorter 
intervals between sessions) docs not always enhance the effectiveness of strength development, this becoming 
effective only later, as strength fitness increases.
This principle may be illustrated by referring to the training results of weightlifters. Exercises with 45-60% 
of 1  RM in the first 8 sessions are slightly more effective than exercises with 60-75% and 75-90% of 1RM loads. 
After 16 sessions, the most effective load was 75-90% of 1RM, whereas the least effective was 45-60% of 1RM 
(Zimkin, 1961). A noticeable strengthening effect occurs for novices using 30-46% of 1 RM, whereas more 
experienced athletes need to use at least 60% of 1RM (Muller & Hettinger, 1957).
To interpret these factors, one must bear in mind the phasic nature of the response to intense strength loads, 
characterised by a temporary decrease in strength and speed of movement, and the subsequent increase in strength 
and speed after the intensity of the resistance has decreased. Therefore, the effectiveness o f heavy weights does 
not occur immediately, but some time later. It has been shown that strength increases well after sessions of 
isometric tension have ceased (Clarke, 1954), while a marked increase in strength and speed of movement from the 
use of sufficient resistance occurs only after at least 20 training sessions (Chemyavsky, 1966).
An increase averaging 18-25% in speed-strcngth for a controlled movement was noted after a 10 day rest 
from intense specialised strength training (Nyeniskin, 1974). It may be assumed that this phenomenon is 
connected with the well-known adaptive inertia of the body and supercompensatory restoration (adaptive 
reconstruction) after strength work.
As strength and level of physical fitness increase, dependence of the increase in strength and its effect on the 
type of training becomes more apparent (with reference to the given means and methods). In those cases where 
training is conducted with small loads, there is a concurrent increase in endurance and speed of movement, along 
with the increase in strength, under loaded and unloaded conditions. If large loads are used in training, strength in­
creases significantly, as does the speed of explosive movement. However, endurance under unloaded conditions 
begins to diminish and can even drop below initial levels.
The magnitude of strength increase and its specific character are also determined by the combination of the 
training means used. For instance, the increase in strength and speed of movement after 20 training sessions in 
which weights of 10% of 1  RM and 40% of 1  RM were used (in different volumes) were as follows: in the group 
whose training volume consisted of 20% with the 10% of I RM load and 80% with the 40% of 1  RM load, there 
was an increase in strength of 44.8% and an increase of 35.2% in the speed of movement from the initial levels. 
The corresponding figures for the second group doing the reverse combination (20% with 40% of 1RM and 80% 
with 10% of 1  RM) were 31.6% and 18.3% respectively (Chemyavsky, 1966).
The increase in strength also depends upon the athlete's level of initial strength fitness. In principle, the lower 
the trainee's level of strength, the greater its increase with training. Virtually all training means prove to be

beneficial in this ease. However, with increase in proficiency, the rate of strength increase diminishes and can be 
elicited only through sufficiently demanding special means of training.
Developing effective methods of strength training involves maintaining the strength already gained. If the 
main goal in the preparatory period is strength development, then it is important that as much strength as 
possible survives into the competition period. In other words, some of the training intensity should be directed at 
preserving the level of strength attained, which is preferable to restoring strength after it has diminished markedly. 
Unfortunately, there are few studies in this area. After 1-2 months without systematic strength work, the 
strength of the extensor muscles decreases by 5-6% and the flexors by 15-20% in skiers. This is especially true 
of athletes who possess a high level of strength development (Chistyakov, 1965). Muscles can lose up to 30% 
of their strength after a period of total (bed) rest of only one week (Muller, 1966). The loss of strength caused by 
complete cessation of resistance training occurs at approximately the same rate as it is increased by training 
(Hettinger & Muller, 1955; Ravick & Larsen, 1959). Moreover, even if strength level does not decrease, heavy 
strength training after a lay-off from exercise for a period of as little as 7-10 days may result in pronounced 
muscle soreness and an inability to maintain training intensity until full recovery has occurred.
The almost total loss of additional strength which was originally produced by 20 sessions of speed-strength 
exercises was noted 5 months after the special training had ceased (8.8% after the first month, 33.8% after the 
second, 60.2% after the third, 81.5% after the fourth and 88.8% after the fifth month). The greatest loss was 
between the second and fourth months (Chenyavsky, 1966). However, according to other data, strength acquired 
over a period of 40 sessions does not decrease to initial levels even a year after training has ceased (Vasiliev, 1954; 
McMorris & Eklins, 1954). A significant proportion of the increase in strength achieved as a result of ten 
electrostimulation sessions was maintained for 5 months (Khvilon, 1974). It has been noted that an increase in 
strength is maintained for a longer period o f time when it is accompanied by an increase in muscle mass 
(DeLorme, 1950; Khrolon, 1974).
Although the above findings give an idea of the general tendencies for the increase and maintenance of 
muscular strength, there are obvious contradictions. Devising reliable methods of special strength preparation 
requires the application of scientific methods to:
• Study the training effect of the means used for a given sport at given levels of fitness
• Determine the optimum sequence, interrelation and continuity of training means for the yearly and multi­
year training periods for different sports and purposes.
Thus, the combination of teaching efforts and special practice should introduce the quantitative programme via the 
basic scheme of special strength training depicted in Figure 4.1, where A, B and C are training means of 
successively greater training effect for a given athlete. In this respect, it should be noted that:
• The contribution of different training means to developing the key motor abilities diminishes with 
improvement in athletic results
• These means are different in terms of their training effect and the use of each of them is justified only when 
the athlete's level of fitness is taken into consideration.
In other words, with growth in sporting proficiency, it is necessary to determine the sequence for introducing the 
chosen means into the training process by calculating the growth and continuity of their training effect. This 
forms the basis for the progressive increase in special work capacity.

4.1.2 The Effect of the Strength Training Means
In recent years scientific research and years of practical experience have yielded a wealth of findings on whka 
current methods of special strength training are based. However, it is necessary to note that this material s I 
generalised and its analysis is theoretical. Although today's athletes attain a high level of sport proficiency, then I 
is still no basis to state that this is the result of a precise methodology of special strength training. To a grot 
extent they achieve proficiency through a large volume of strength work and a colossal expenditure of energy. 
Generally, the selection and use of means for organising special strength training has a number of weaknesses.
Despite its apparent diversity, the range of special strength training means is rather limited. In effect 
beginners and highly qualified athletes use essentially the same means, the difference being largely in the volum e 
and intensity of their loads.
Firstly, this leads to training monotony and secondly, the body adapts to a repeated stimulus and doeswx 
respond with the desired level of adaptation. Qualified athletes therefore spend much time using ineffective 
means, none of which improves their level of strength fitness. Beginners, on the other hand, often use vigorous ' 
overloading methods for which they are not yet prepared and disrupt the natural process of achieving spon 
mastery.
An essential shortcoming in the organisation of strength training is that athletes pay little attention to the 
phenomenon of the qualitative specificity of the training effect of strength exercises. Therefore, very often they 
use means whose specific training effect relates only weakly to the demands placed upon the body by the 
fundamental exercises. For instance, exercises that are selected for strength development often offer only general 
conditioning.
At the other extreme, there is the attempt to select exercises which are structurally similar to the fundamental 
exercises. This may be justified under certain circumstances, but it is sometimes carried to absurd lengths and 
athletes devise such intricate exercises that they are even less effective than traditional general conditioning 
movements. This reveals that any system of special training is deficient if it arbitrarily combines general 
developmental and special strength exercises.
In order to devise a sound scientific system it is necessary to evaluate objectively the training effect of the 
strength means. The training effect is result of the influence of a means or complex of means on the body as 
revealed by the magnitude, quality and stability of the resulting adaptive changes. A number of specific factors 
which reflect the training effect are examined for selecting the training means and devising a methodical system of 
special strength preparation.
It is first of all necessary to distinguish (see 6.7.1) between the acute (immediate) training effect (ATE) and 
the delayed training effect (DTE). The body's immediate reaction to the application of a strength means is 
expressed in a short-term improvement of or deterioration in the athlete's current functional state. Deterioration 
or improvement depends upon the energy cost of the task, which determines the rest interval prior to execution of 
the next exercise: it may be increased if the body requires more rest or be optimally shortened if the superimposed 
after-effect phenomenon is exploited beneficially by the body. The negative reaction of the body is thus removed, 
as revealed by its relatively stable adaptation, which is substantial only if the volume of the training influence is 
sufficient.
The particular effect and cumulative effect are the result of the use of one or more unidirectional means or a 
complex of multi-directional means. In the first case, the adaptation reflects the specificity of the means used in 
the given regime. In the second case, the adaptation displays an integrated, generalised character. However, this is 
not simply the sum of the body's functional changes, but a complex of new forms of its motor potential which 
contains the specific characteristics of the particular training means.
The athlete's success depends largely upon the skill to select a diverse spectrum of exercise means which will 
produce the required cumulative training effect. One should also take into consideration factors that are 
characteristic of the training effect, such as absolute and relative strength, muscular endurance, stability and 
temporal features. It is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of two or more means in order to select the one 
which produces the optimal increase in absolute strength. The qualitative and quantitative characteristics of the 
training effect provide measures of its specific form and the magnitude of improvement in performance. Finally, 
the stability and temporal characteristics of the training effect are evaluated by the length of time for which it is 
maintained.
